HELD: There are number of works entrusted by IIT Bhubaneswar to the applicant under a single contract/agreement made on 2-5-2016. It is also found that IIT,Bhubaneswar has engaged the applicant as a 'Project Management Consultant'. In order to execute the project, the applicant has engaged contractors through different competitive tender process. The applicant has awarded different types of works to various agencies/contractors with categorical mention of individual works to be carried out by them with specific remuneration for each such work. Hence, it is a supply having distinctly identifiable components with distinct value attributable to each of the components. However, the contention of the applicant cannot be agreed with for the reasons that the items covered under the 'Scope of Work' are disjoint in character and can be supplied in conjunction with each other in the ordinary course of business. Hence, the views of the applicant that the supply of services and goods encompassed in the subject work order/contract are naturally bundled cannot be accepted. Mere fact that a number of tasks have been entrusted to the applicant would not make it entitled to be categorised as 'composite supply' particularly in terms of section 2(30). [Para 4.2]

The applicant has stated that IIT, Bhubaneswar has been established by the Government. All the institutions of the Indian Institutes of Technology are established by the Government of India, Ministry of Human Resource Development. Further, IITs under the All India Council of Technical Education (AICTE) are the institutions controlled and owned by the Ministry of Human Resource Development. That being the stated position, IIT, Bhubaneswar is entitled to be termed as 'Government Entity' in terms of Explanation to Notification No. 11/2017 - C.T. (Rate), and also as per Notification No. 31/2017 - C.T. (Rate), dated 13-10-2017. The issue of IIT, Bhubaneswar being a Government entity has been stated with at length in the application submitted by the Applicant. 'Government Entity' is defined in the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax rate vide clause 4(x). [Para 4.3]

Government of India, Ministry of Human Resource Development is exercising full control over the activities of IITs all over the country. In the given circumstance IIT, Bhubaneswar qualifies to be called and termed as a 'Government Entity' for the purpose of GST law, as it fulfils the necessary and sufficient conditions laid down under notification supra. It therefore leaves no doubt that IIT, Bhubaneswar is a Government Entity for the purpose of provisions of CGST Act, 2017 and OGST Act, 2017. [Para 4.4]

Entry No. 3(vi) to the Notification No. 11/2017-C.T. (R) covers a wide spectrum of Construction Services as composite supply. [Para 4.5]

In the instant case it is found that the applicant has been engaged as a PMC to execute the contract for carrying out different specified works for IIT, Bhubaneswar which includes erection, commissioning, installation, etc. It is also found that for executing the project, the applicant shall be paid agency charges of 5.5 per cent in addition to the actual cost of work. The agency charges are type of commission or remuneration for rendering 'consulting service' to IIT, Bhubaneswar. I am planning to construct a residential complex with more than twelve houses. I plan to give them on rent to various persons. I have given contract to a contractor to build the complex for me. Should the contractor charge service tax from me? The service of residential complex is not taxable if the residential complex is intended for personal use as residence. As per Explanation ( a) to section 65(91a ), ‘personal use’ includes permitting the complex for use as residence by another person on rent or without consideration. Thus, in your case, the service is not taxable.

The question will arise if you after some time, decide to sell the flats instead of giving these on rent. In such case, the service tax cannot be levied, as what is important is the nature of service at the time of providing service. Subsequent events cannot change the nature of service provided, particularly when the words used are ‘intended for personal use’ and not ‘used for personal residence’.

When construction of residential complex services can be treated as ‘export of service’ for exemption of service tax ?

In case of construction of residential complex services, the service will be ‘export of service’ only if - (a) the immovable property is situated abroad, (b) the service is delivered outside India and used in business or for any other purpose outside India and (c) payment for such service is received in convertible, i.e., free foreign exchange.

What is the value for purpose of calculation of service tax?

Service tax is payable on gross amount charged for service provided or to be provided.

Often contract for construction of complex is a compo-site contract, i.e., inclusive of material cost. In such cases, instead of identifying value of taxable services in a composite contract, tax on service of construction of residential complex can be paid on 33 per cent of gross amount charged. This would be so if (a) the gross amount charged includes value of goods and materials supplied or provided or used by provider of the construction service for providing such service and (b) Cenvat credit of inputs and capital goods is not availed. This simple method is not available in case of only completion and finishing services (Notification No. 18/2005-ST dated June 7, 2005).

Is there a simple method to pay service tax?

A service provider providing taxable service of construction of residential complex can opt to pay service tax on 33 per cent of gross amount charged. The gross amount should include value of goods and materials supplied or provided or used. However, he can avail this concession only if - (a) He does not avail Cenvat of duty paid on inputs and capital goods (He can avail Cenvat of input services) and (b) He does not avail benefit of Notification No. 12/2003-ST dated June 20, 2003 and Notification No. 18/2005-ST dated June 7, 2005.

This simple method is not available in case the service provider provides only completion and finishing services (as in such cases, material content will be much less).

The partial exemption is available only if the gross amount charged includes value of goods and materials supplied or provided or used by provider of the commercial or industrial construction service for providing such service [Explanation to Notification No. 18/2005-ST]. Thus, if the customer provides some material, its value will have to be added for purpose of payment of service tax.

As per Notification No. 12/2003-ST, no service tax is payable on value of material or goods sold to recipient of service. Thus, if a service provider avails exemption under 15/2004-ST, he cannot avail concessional rate of 33 per cent of gross amount charged to customers.

The service provider can have benefit either under No. 12/2003-ST or No. 15/2004-ST and not both.

Requirement of completion certificate

GST would be levied if amount is received prior to completion certificate (or occupation) and there would be no GST if the entire amount is received after the completion certificate.

It can be seen that similar provisions exist in service tax in regard to requirement of completion certificate for exclusion of a property from levy of tax. However, there is a difference in the provisions for such requirement. While in Service Tax, issuance of completion certificate is required for exclusion of property from levy of tax, however in GST, property will be excluded at the time of:

Issuance of completion certificate by the competent authority, if required; or

After its first occupation

Whichever is earlier.

Thus, in case of GST property will be excluded, even if it occupied by people and no completion certificate is received. As per the said scheme, a separate Section (Section 5: Construction Services) has been provided for the Construction service which is further sub-divided into headings and groups. Developers need to ascertain their category and SAC for various purposes under GST regime.

Valuation

Valuation of the services would be at the transaction value. However, valuation with the related parties/ between various group companies needs to be properly dealt with and must be kept at the arm's length price to avoid unnecessary departmental intrusion.

However, one major change has been done in the valuation provisions in GST. In real estate sector, generally customer delays in making to the payment to the developers. Many times, the developer charges interest on such delayed payment. Such interest is outside the scope of tax net presently as no tax is charged on such interest whether it be VAT, Service Tax or Excise Duty. However, in GST regime, such interest will be included in the transaction value of supply and accordingly GST will be levied on such interest. Further, builder will need to bifurcate the interest on basic construction amount and amount of other services like PLC etc. as interest on basic amount will be chargeable at the rate of 12% (i.e. rate of main supply) and interest on other services at 18%.

Treatment of cancellations of bookings

In real estate sector, cancellations of bookings of flats/shops etc. is a very prevalent and common practice. Since the delivery period of a project is very high often extending to several years, many customers cancel their bookings of flats during the project.

Presently, developers can issue credit note and take benefit under Rule 6(3) of Service Tax Rules, 1994, in regard to the tax paid earlier on a cancelled booking when such booking is cancelled. Similar provisions exist in VAT laws also.

Same concept has been kept in GST regime, wherein a person can issue a credit note in case of cancellation of a service and take benefit of the tax paid earlier on such service. However, as per Section 34 of CGST Act, 2017, such credit note have to be shown/declared in the return of the month when such note is issued. However, there is a restriction which says that such credit note can be shown only up to in the return for the month of September of the following financial year in which supply is made.

Illustration

Suppose a supply was made in the month of August, 2017(F.Y. 2017-18). If a credit note is issued against this transaction, it can be shown in any return up to return of the month of September' 2018 (F.Y. 2018-19). However, if any credit note is issued after this date, it cannot be shown in return and therefore, its benefit cannot be taken.

This provision is going to pose a major hurdle for real estate sector because the construction projects usually take several years to complete. Therefore, various customers book their flats and then cancels the booking several many months/years later. However, the benefit will be available only for a selected period and would pose a very troublesome issue.

Exemption for construction industry withdrawn

Earlier, in service tax, Central Government has provided many construction service related exemption like construction of canal, dams, road, affordable housing projects etc. But, with the introduction of GST regime, government is looking to end this Exemption-Raj of service tax for many construction related services. Now, in GST, only pure labour contracts entered for house construction under Housing for All(Urban) Mission/Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY) and labour contracts used in construction of single residential unit otherwise than as a part of residential complex are kept exempt as per draft exemption list released by the GST council.

Major impact will be on affordable housing projects which are currently exempt from service tax and have not been kept in the exemption list of GST.

Flow of credits

In present regime, a Builder opting for Abatement under Notification No. 26/2012-ST is not eligible for CENVAT credit of inputs (Excise Duty). In GST regime, all the above duties/taxes (except stamp duty) will get subsumed, therefore a builder will be able to avail the input tax credit of all its procurement of goods/services. Therefore, it would reduce the tax costs substantially in the construction industry. Notification No. 31/2017 - CT (Rate), dated 13/10/2017 defines the terms 'Governmental Authority' and 'Government Entity' under para 4(ix) and (x) respectively. Both refer inter alia to an authority set up by an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature with 90 per cent or more participation by way of equity or control. The Governmental Authority, however, is established to carry out functions entrusted to a Municipality or Panchayat under Art 243W or 243G of the Constitution respectively: whereas, a Government Entity is set up to carry out any function entrusted by the Central Government, State Government, Union Territory or local authority. According to the objects and reasons of the IWAI Act, 1985, the IWAI is an Authority set up for 'the regulation and development of inland waterways for the purpose of shipping and navigation and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.' The Central Government appoints and removes members of the IWAI, provides grants and loans, sanctions projects, gives directions, makes rules, and can supersede the Authority if required. The IWAI is thus a statutory authority under direct control of the Central Government. It is, therefore, a 'Government Entity' in terms of para 4(x) of Notification No. 31/2017 - CT (Rate), dated 13-10-2017. Letter of the GST Council highlights this status of the IWAI. [Para 4]

GST is payable at the rate of 12 per cent on supply of works contract service to a Government Entity, which is pointed out in the Council's above-mentioned letter. However, it is subject to the terms and conditions of Serial No. 3 (vi) of the Rate Notification, as described above. The concession under Serial No. 3 (vi) of the Rate Notification is contract specific. The recipient Government Entity should procure the works contract service in relation to a work entrusted to it by the Central Government, State Government, Union territory or local authority, as the case may be. If it is not covered under Serial No. 3(vi) (b) or 3(vi) (c ), it should be a civil structure or an original work meant predominantly for use other than for commerce, industry, or any other business or profession [Serial No. 3(vi)(a)]. [Para 5]

Section 14(1)(b) of the IWAI Act, 1985 empowers IWAI to set up infrastructural facilities for national waterways. No such projects, however, can be undertaken without approval from the Central Government unless the amount involved is below a threshold [2nd proviso to section 13 and section 14(4) of the IWAI Act, 1985]. Therefore, construction of multi-modal IWT Terminal, involving Rs. 517.36 crores, if lawfully contracted, is a project undertaken within the functional authority entrusted to IWAI and with Govt sanction, satisfying the condition under column (5) of the Serial No. 3(vi) of the Rate Notification. [Para 6]

The provision has been very clumsily drafted. Hence, we have to understand the provision considering the principle behind the provisions.

What is written below is not what is actually written against Sr Nos. 41A and 41B but what is actually meant (based on principles). Hope the notification will be amended suitably to clarify the position.

As per the principle, the first step is to calculate GST payable on development rights transferred, which pertain to residential apartments.

(A) GST on transfer of development rights/FST attributable residential apartments = GST payable on TDR or FSI (including additional FSI) or both or on upfront amount payable in respect of service by way of granting of long term lease of thirty years, or more for construction of the project] × (carpet area of the residential apartments in the project) ÷ (Total carpet area of the residential and commercial apartments in the project) .

[The notification wrongly terms it as 'Amount of exemption available for construction of residential apartments].

The second step is to calculate GST payable by promoter on un-booked residential apartments.

The promoter shall be liable to pay tax at the applicable rate, on reverse charge basis, on such proportion of value of development rights or FSI (Including additional FSI) or both, or upfront amount (called as premium, salami, cost, price, development charges or by any other name) paid for long term lease of land, as is attributable to the residential apartments, which remain un-booked on the date of issuance of completion certificate, or first occupation of the project, as the case may be.

The calculation will be made in the following manner -

(B) GST payable on residential apartments remain un-booked on date of completion = [GST payable on TDR or FSI (including additional FSI) or both or upfront amount (called as premium, salami, cost, price, development charges or by any other name) payable for long term lease of land for construction of the residential apartments in the project but for the exemption contained herein] × (carpet area of the residential apartments in the project which remain un-booked on the date of issuance of completion certificate or first occupation÷ Total carpet area of the residential apartments in the project) - first proviso to Sr Nos. 41A and 41B of Notification No. 12/2019-CT (Rate) dated 28-6-2017 inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2019.

The exemption available on transfer of development rights/FSI attributable to residential apartments which were booked prior to date of completion = (A) - (B).

Upper limit for tax on residential apartments - The tax payable in terms of above shall not exceed 0.5% of CGST (plus 0.5% of SGST/UTGST) of the value in case of affordable residential apartments and 2.5% of CGST (plus 2.5% of SGST/UTGST) of the value in case of residential apartments other than affordable residential apartments remaining un-booked on the date of issuance of completion certificate or first occupation - first part of second proviso to Sr Nos. 41A and 41B of Notification No. 12/2019-CT (Rate) dated 28-6-2017 inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2019.

Time when liability of promoter arises - The liability to pay central tax on the said portion of the development rights or FSI, or both, or upfront amount paid for long term lease of land, calculated as above, shall arise on the date of completion or first occupation of the project, as the case may be, whichever is earlier - second part of second proviso to Sr Nos. 41A and 41B of Notification No. 12/2019-CT (Rate) dated 28-6-2017 inserted w.e.f. 1-4-2019.

23.1-1 Statutory provisions in respect of construction of complex

Following is 'supply of service' as per para 5(b) of Schedule II of CGST Act.

Construction of a complex, building, civil structure or a part thereof, including a complex or building intended for sale to a buyer, wholly or partly, except where the entire consideration has been received after issuance of completion certificate, where required, by the competent authority or after its first occupation, whichever is earlier.

Explanation.- For the purposes of this clause- (1) the expression "competent authority" means the Government or any authority authorized to issue completion certificate under any law for the time being in force and in case of non-requirement of such certificate from such authority, from any of the following, namely - (i) an architect registered with the Council of Architecture constituted under the Architects Act, 1972; or (ii) a chartered engineer registered with the Institution of Engineers (India); or (iii) a licensed surveyor of the respective local body of the city or town or village or development or planning authority.

(2) the expression "construction" includes additions, alterations, replacements or remodeling of any existing civil structure.

Residential Complex - "Residential complex" means any complex comprising of a building or buildings, having more than one single residential unit - para 2 of Notification No. 12/2017-CT (Rate) and No. 9/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 28-6-2017, effective from 1-7-2017.

Single Residential Unit - "Single residential unit" means a self-contained residential unit which is designed for use, wholly or principally, for residential purposes for one family - para 2 of Notification No. 12/2017-CT (Rate) and No. 9/2017-IT (Rate) both dated 28-6-2017, effective from 1-7-2017.

Occupancy certificate granted in is equal to completion certificate - In Mumbai i.e. Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC), occupancy certificate is granted. Sale after such occupancy certificate (even before completion certificate) will be sale of immovable property and outside service tax net - PIB (Press Information Bureau), Ministry of Finance dated 26-10-2015.

Same view has been held in Bindu Ventures, In re [2018] 100 taxmann.com 207 (AAR - Karnataka) in respect of occupancy certificate issued by Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike.

23.1-2 Meaning of 'first occupation'

As per para 5 of Schedule III read with para 5(b) of Schedule II of CGST Act, If entire consideration is received 'after issuance of completion certificate/occupancy certificate by the competent authority or its first occupation whichever is earlier', the promoter (builder or developer) is not liable to pay GST, even if completion certificate or occupancy certificate is not obtained from authorities.

The words 'after its first occupation' are confusing. 'Occupation' by whom? The 'occupation' should be of that particular apartment which is being sold or any apartment in that complex?

SERVICE PROVIDED TO ONE OF UNIT IN A RESIDENTIAL COMPLEX Mr. ‘A’ provides services of painting of commercial and residential units, polishing of wooden doors, windows and frames of doors and windows. Mr. ‘B’ appoints Mr. ‘A’ to paint his residential unit and polish wooden doors and frames of doors and windows, etc. Mr. ‘B’ utilizes this residential unit for personal use (He resides in it). This residential unit of Mr. ‘B’ is situated in a society building containing more than 100 such residential units and occupied by different persons. Kindly guide whether service tax is attracted on this service and Mr. ‘A’ is liable to pay Service Tax ? If not, what documents Mr. ‘A’ has to take from Mr. ‘B’ to prove that he is not liable to pay service tax on this service.

In my view, A is liable to pay service tax since it is a residential complex and painting, etc., is certainly in relation to repairs, alteration, renovation or restoration of residential complex. It will be so even if the contract is only for one unit.

ONE CONTRACTOR CONSTRUCTING 11 FLATS

If there are 44 flats in a residential project and 4 contractors are hired for 11 flats each, are they liable to service tax ?

As per section 65(30a), effective from June 16, 2005, ‘construction of complex’ means—(a) construction of a new residential complex or a part thereof. . . .

Thus, in this case, it is a full ‘residential complex’ and 11 flats is ‘part thereof’ and hence service tax will apply.

DIGGING AND PLANTING TREES IN CONSTRUCTION AREA

A contractor is providing service for digging and planting trees in an industrial construction area. Whether he is liable for service tax ? If yes, under which head ?

It can come under site formation and clearance service if it is prior to construction. If the service is after construction is over, it may not come under any specific head.

SEPARATE CONSTRUCTION AGREEMENT WITH EACH BUYER

When a builder, carrying a project of 18 bungalows, makes a sale agreement for the land and enters into a separate contract for construction of each bungalow with 18 different people, whether he is liable for service tax ? Further, the builder gives contracts for the same to 2 different contractors for 9 bungalows each. Whether in this case contractor is liable for the service tax ?

In both cases, answer is ‘Yes’, since it is a ‘part of residential complex’

DEVELOPING LAND FOR SOCIETY

A society has purchased land. It has given following work to a developer - (1) divide into plots (2) build internal roads, garden, etc. Is the service taxable?

It can come under site formation and clearance services. See CBE&C clarification, which seems to be legally tenable.

The definition of ‘site formation and clearance, excavation and earthmoving and demolition’ is an inclusive definition and the activities specifically mentioned are indicative and not exhaustive. Prior to construction of buildings, factory or any civil structure, activity of mining or laying of cables or pipes, preparation services of site formation and clearance, excavation and earthmoving or levelling are normally undertaken for a consideration to make the land suitable for such activities. All such activities fall within the scope of this service paras 6.2 to 6.4 of MF(DR) Circular No. B1/6/2005-TRU, dated July 27, 2005.

ANNUAL INCENTIVE EARNED BY DISTRIBUTOR

I am a distributor for some companies and have a contractual agreement with them, and on the same I get annual incentives (based on turnover only) I may purchase as and when required. Can service tax department ask for service tax under head ‘promotion’ under BAS for annual incentive ?

You have to go by predominant nature of contract. If predominant nature of contract is sale and purchase, then it is not service contract, as service, if any, is only incidental. Any dealer or shopkeeper will make efforts to increase the sales of products of Principal (as his turnover increases). That does not mean that he is prompting sale of goods of Principal. In fact, he is promoting his own sales.

Are services provided to RBI exempt ?

No.

The Floor Area Ratio (FAR), also known as the Floor Space Ratio (FSR) or the Floor Space Index (FSI), depicts the relationship between the total usable floor space in a building and the total area of the plot on which the building is constructed. In mathematical terms, FAR = CA/LA, where CA = Constructed area or built-up area, and LA = Land area. [Para 4.8] According to the Project Plan submitted at the time of the hearing, FAR for the entire project is 2.749 after deducting from the total built-up area the common areas like lift-lobby, stair area etc. FAR for the affordable residential apartments in the project should, therefore, be atleast 1.375. The total plot size being 5627 sq. mtr., the built-up area for affordable residential apartments should atleast be 7734 sq. mtr. The built-up area for the affordable residential apartments, as identified by the architect, under the RREP is 7885 sq. mtr. (the calculation sheet is attached). The relevant FAR, therefore, comes out to be 1.401, which is 50.96 per cent of the FAR for the project. The RREP, therefore, is an affordable housing project in terms of the AHP Notification. [Para 4.9]

AMC FOR ONE YEAR

We entered into an AMC for one year. During the year, service tax rate was increased from 10 per cent to 12 per cent. Is it necessary to pay service tax for the balance period on pro rata basis? In my view, it can be argued that the entire service is provided as soon as the AMC is entered into. Hence, difference in service tax should not be payable. For example, in case of insurance, when the policy is issued, risk for entire year is covered. Hence, rate of service tax as applicable as on date of issue of policy should be applicable – a view prima facie expressed in Bajaj Allianz General Insurance Co. v. CCE [2007] 9 STT 446 (CESTAT - Mum.). Same principle should apply in case of AMC also.

JOB WORKER MANUFACTURING EXEMPTED PRODUCT

We are in process of engaging a Job worker for manufacturing of Fruit Pulp or Fruit juice base drinks falling under the Chapter heading 2202 90 20 attracting 16 per cent Tariff rate and effective rate of duty is Nil vide Notification No. 3/2006-CE, dated March 1, 2006. All the required raw material will be given by us and the Job worker will manufacture the above product under our brand name and sell to us charging conversion charges. The final product after receiving at our depot will be sold to the consumer. Whether the job worker is liable to pay service tax under the category of Business Auxiliary Service or can he claim exemption under Notification No. 8/2005-S.T., dated March 1, 2005?

Really, if an activity is ‘manufacture’, it is outside the definition of ‘Business Auxiliary Service’. There is no provision that duty should have been paid on it. Of course, the department may not take it so easily, and job worker will have to fight it out (of course indirectly you have to support him). It is advisable to inform all details in advance to department to avoid charge of suppression of facts.

CONSTRUCTION SERVICES

I booked an office from one of the developers of commercial complex about two years back. Now the developer is demanding service tax on the total booking price on the plea that service tax has been levied. My query is whether the service tax is leviable on the total cost of office (as it also includes a major portion as cost of land) or only on the construction cost of superstructure?

Actually, sale of ready flat is not ‘construction service’. ‘Construction of service’ comes into picture only when you enter into a contract for construction. In such case, actually, after construction, there is no sale deed. Only undivided land is transferred to you. Thus, if your contract was for sale of flat, there is no service tax. In any case, service tax cannot be on value of land. It can be only on value of construction.

One of My client is constructing residential quarters for CPWD which is to be used by CRPF for their employees. CPWD after construction will hand it over to CRPF and which would be given by CRPF to its employees at concessional rent or else no rent would be charged from them (free of cost), but it any case the quarters would be neither sold nor transferred to the users. The issue which need to be examined in this case is whether service tax is leviable on such constructions where the construction is intended to be used for personal use as defined under the section which creates charge under ‘Construction of Residential Complex Services’.

Really, the construction is for ‘personal use’, the only hitch is that it is not for personal use of ‘CPWD’, but of CRPF. The contractor has got order from CPWD and not from CRPF. However, legally, CPWD and CRPF is one legal entity, i.e., the Government. They are not two legal entities though for administrative purposes, they function separately. You have to check what is the arrangement between CRPF and CPWD. Even if CRPF is paying for it, these do not become two legal entities. From that angle, in my view, it will be ‘residential purpose’. It is advisable to inform department in writing to avoid subsequent harassment.

The applicants are constructing civil structure to house various equipment, electrical installation, infrastructure, etc. Their work involves Construction buildings for housing the equipment room, Data centers, Nearline data centers, Disaster Recovery Center, Training of Project Management Team, Supply of Equipment at a central site of bidder and segregrated as per site, Staging of Equipment, Joint Testing, Delivery of Equipment to sites, Installation of equipment, Certification of Network by a Certifying Authority, Commissioning of the Network, Training for trainers and Completion of Warranty.

Thus the contract is for a surveillance system to be put into place for which the most important items are the equipments which are requires for the system to function. This is the principal requirement and after supply of these equiments the same are required to be put to use. Hence, the equipments have to be installed, connected with wires to various components etc, as submitted by the applicant and since the same cannot be kept in the open they are to be housed in buildings consisting of operational areas, etc.

It is found from the proposed contracts that the tender is intended to setup a Next Generation Network which will support net-centric operations a key enabler for the administrative operations/war fighting operations of the Indian Navy. The term 'original works' as defined in Notification No. 12/2017 covers activities in the nature of erection, commissioning or installation of machinery or structure. The scope of the subject proposed contract necessitates the applicant to build structures in the form of buildings, roads, etc. and undertake the activity of installing the equipment therein, etc. However it is found that the equipments which are installed by the applicant are first supplied by them. Thus, it is seen that it is not a fact that the applicants are only involved in erection, commissioning or installation of machinery belonging to some other person but are installing and commissioning the equipments supplied by them. Hence, primarily what they are doing is supplying goods i.e. equipments. Thus, the works to be undertaken by them cannot be considered as 'original work'.

The applicant has made submissions to support their contention that the subject contract should be considered as falling under clause (vi) (a) of section 5 of Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended. However, in view of the discussions it is found that the subject contract does not envisage original works and it is also seen that the contract is not in respect of a civil structure. Hence, it is found that the applicant's contention cannot be accepted and the said contract does not fall under clause (vi) (a) of section 5 of Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended. It is also seen that the subject contract does not satisfy the descriptions mentioned in clauses (i) to (xii) except clause (ii) of section 5 of Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended.

The subject work to be undertaken by the applicant is a composite supply of works contract, since it includes supply of both, goods and services and does not fall in any of the clauses (i) to (xii) except clause (ii) of section 5 of Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate) as amended. Hence, the subject contract is taxable and the tax rate to be applied is 18 percent GST. [Para 5]

Thus, the supply of goods or services for 'setting up of network' would qualify as a Composite supply of works contract as defined in clause (119) of section 2 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017.

The rate of tax applicable to the supplies will be 18 per cent GST. [Para 6]

Nowadays, realty sector is on full boom. So the question that arises for consideration is that; whether realtor constructing building by taking booking amount from prospective buyers, will also be covered under this category and liable for Service Tax? The CBEC has clarified the issue in its consolidated master circular in the following manner: Thus as per this clarification if builder/promoter/developer undertakes construction work on his own without engaging the services of any other person, it is not taxable. But Sub-contractors providing the construction services (to main contractor or to any other person) will be liable to pay service tax. But a recent ruling given by the Authority for Advance Ruling has created furore in the realty sector, which is facing the financial crunch in the recent time. One of the significant factors which result in negative ruling against the applicant was specification of particular flats at the time of booking. But it is not clear whether just booking in advance without specifying particular flat, would have changed the ruling. Though the ruling of Authority for Advance Ruling has only persuasive value and is not binding on other assessees, but the Service Tax Department may try to take the benefit of this ruling. The views of the experts are also divided on this ruling.

Decision of Authority for Advance Rulings in the case of Harekrishna Developers, In re [2008] 14 STT 53 (AAR - New Delhi)

2.2 Facts

The applicant-firm wants to develop a residential housing complex on its own land at its own expense. The applicant will book the residential unit in favour of a particular buyer after taking a token booking amount. The physical possession of the residential unit will be given to the buyer after construction is completed and full payment is received. At the time of booking, the customers enter into agreement that building and development of the residential units and common facilities/amenities are to be done by the applicant. The construction material will be bought by the applicant. A part of the said complex will be constructed by the applicant itself and rest through contractors. The applicant sought advance ruling of the Authority on the questions as to whether the activity, which is to be undertaken by the applicant is a taxable service and to what extent it is liable to pay service tax?

Decision of Authority for Advance Ruling

1. The Authority for Advance Ruling observed that the complex to be constructed by the applicant conforms to the definition of ‘residential complex’ which is meant for sale to the prospective buyers as part of the applicant’s business activity. As explicitly laid down in clause (91a) of section 65, it does not include a complex which is constructed by a person directly engaging the services of any other person for designing or planning of the layout, if it is meant to be used for residential purpose either by him or his lessee or a person permitted by him. Such a construction gets excluded from the purview of the residential complex and does not, therefore, fall either within the ambit of sub-clause (zzzh) or clause (ii)(c ) of Explanation to sub-clause (zzzza). In contrast, where the owner of the land instead of directly building the house with the assistance of an architect or engineer, entrusts the construction work to a contractor, there is a clear liability on the part of the contractor to pay service tax because he becomes service provider in relation to the execution of the works contract entrusted to him.

2. In the absence of any specific provision in the Act on this issue, you have to go by basic principle of law that ‘taxable event’ is ‘provision of service’. On the basis of this principle, service tax will not be payable in respect of services provided prior to 10-9-2004 in case of commercial and industrial complex and prior to 16-6-2005 in case of residential complex. Thus, service tax should be payable on pro rata basis on services provided after 10-9-2004 in case of commercial and industrial complex and after 16-6-2005 in case of residential complex. 3. Value of taxable service

What is the ‘value’ for purpose of levy of service tax?

Service tax is payable on ‘value of services’. Value of service shall be the gross amount charged by the service provider for ‘such’ (i.e. taxable) service provided or to be provided by him - Section 67 of the Finance Act, 1994.

Is there a simple method to pay service tax?

Often contract for construction is a composite contract i.e., inclusive of material cost. Hence, finding value of ‘taxable service’ is very difficult. A contractor can opt for a simplified method, which is clarified by department as follows - (a) Circular No. MF(DR) circular No. B2/8/2004-TRU, dated 10-9-2004 in case of construction of industrial or commercial complex (b) para 13.6 of MF(DR) Circular No. B1/6/2005-TRU, dated 27-7-2005 in respect of residential complex.

Any person providing taxable service of commercial or industrial construction can opt to pay service tax on 33% of gross amount charged. This is at the option of service provider.

The gross amount should include value of goods and materials supplied or provided or used. However, he can avail this concession only if - (a) He does not avail Cenvat of duty/service tax paid on inputs, input services and capital goods and (b) He does not avail benefit of Notification No. 12/2003-ST dated 20‑6‑2003. This relaxation is not available if only completion and finishing services are provided - Notification No. 1/2006-ST, dated 1-3-2006.

As per earlier Notification No. 15/2004-ST, dated 10-9-2004 in respect of commercial or industrial complex and Notification No. 18/2005-ST, dated 7-6-2005 in respect of residential complex, the service provider could avail Cenvat of input services. These notifications have been rescinded w.e.f. 1-3-2006 and now he cannot avail any Cenvat credit at all, if he avails aforesaid abatement.

The partial exemption is available only if the gross amount charged includes value of goods and materials supplied or provided or used by provider of the commercial or industrial construction of service for providing such service (Explanation to Notification No. 1/2006-ST). Thus, if the customer provides some material, its value will have to be added for purpose of payment of service tax.

Entry No. 3(v)(da) of the Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 is related to the construction of low-cost apartments. Clause (xvi) of Paragraph 4 of the Rate Notification defines an affordable residential apartment. It shall mean a residential apartment in a project which commences on or after 1-4-2019 or in an ongoing project in respect of which the promoter has not exercised the option to pay tax at the rate specified in (ie) or (if) of Entry No. 3, having carpet area not exceeding 60 sq. mtr. in metropolitan cities or 90 sq. mtr. In cities or towns other than metropolitan cities and for which the gross amount charged is not more than 45 lakhs. [Para 4.1]

The flats having a carpet area of 60 sq. mtr. or less per unit in the RREP qualify as affordable residential apartments, provided the gross amount charged per unit does not exceed Rs. 45 lakhs and the promoter has not exercised the option to pay tax at the rate specified in (ie) or (if) of Entry No. 3. It now needs to be ascertained whether the RREP is an affordable housing project, which enjoys infrastructure status vide the AHP Notification. [Para 4.6]

Affordable housing has been defined in the AHP Notification as a housing project using at least 50 per cent of FAR/FSI for dwelling units with a carpet area of not more than 60 sq. mtr. The term 'carpet area' has been assigned the same meaning as in section 2(k) of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016. It means the net usable floor area of an apartment, excluding the area covered by the external walls, areas under services shafts, balcony or veranda and open terrace, but includes the area covered by the internal partition walls of the apartment. [Para 4.7]

The Floor Area Ratio (FAR), also known as the Floor Space Ratio (FSR) or the Floor Space Index (FSI), depicts the relationship between the total usable floor space in a building and the total area of the plot on which the building is constructed. In mathematical terms, FAR = CA/LA, where CA = Constructed area or built-up area, and LA = Land area. [Para 4.8]

According to the Project Plan submitted at the time of the hearing, FAR for the entire project is 2.749 after deducting from the total built-up area the common areas like lift-lobby, stair area etc. FAR for the affordable residential apartments in the project should, therefore, be atleast 1.375. The total plot size being 5627 sq. mtr., the built-up area for affordable residential apartments should atleast be 7734 sq. mtr. The built-up area for the affordable residential apartments, as identified by the architect, under the RREP is 7885 sq. mtr. (the calculation sheet is attached). The relevant FAR, therefore, comes out to be 1.401, which is 50.96 per cent of the FAR for the project. The RREP, therefore, is an affordable housing project in terms of the AHP Notification. [Para 4.9]

Thus, it is concluded that the works contract service for the construction of those dwelling units in the RREP that are affordable residential apartments in terms of clause (xvi) of Paragraph 4 of the Rate Notification are taxable under Entry No. 3(v)(da) of the said notification, provided the applicant does not opt for paying tax at the rate specified in (ie) or (if) of Entry No. 3. [Para 4.10]

Thus, the works contract service for the construction of those dwelling units in the project named 'Akriti' that are affordable residential apartments in terms of clause (xvi) of Paragraph 4 of Notification No. 11/2017 - Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017, as amended from time-to-time, are taxable under Entry No. 3(v)(da) of the said notification, provided the applicant does not opt for paying tax at the rate specified in Entry No. 3(ie) or 3(if). [Para 4.10]

QUERIES

TUSHAR K. DOCTOR*

We are doing the turnkey projects in environmental engineering. Our scope of work includes design, supply, erection, and installation and commissioning. Our order is generally composite contract. Payments terms indicate release of payments on basis of completion like certain amount as advance against order, submission of design, drawing, against supply of material, against erection and installation, against commissioning and finally against successful trial run, etc.

QUESTIONS :

1.What basic precaution is required to be taken while submitting tender or accepting the order from client keeping in view the implication of service tax ?

2.If order is composite, is it required to mention in the order the value of the various activities like Supply, Design and Drawing, Erection, Installation and Commissioning, etc., to ascertain the service tax obligation ? Is there any way to save the service tax by doing proper presentation in the order and bills, etc. What is that ?

3.We are already registered with Excise Department, Service Tax Cell, for our Consulting Engineer, Installation and Commissioning and Repairs and Maintenance. In the said Registration billing address is from our Registered office, i.e., A-116, whereas we are doing project all over India and registered under Sales Tax Act in each State wherever we are doing the project. In such situation we are billing from each of such States directly to the client. So what is the alternative with regard to billing for service tax in such case ?

4.As the rate of service tax has been increased from 8 per cent to 10.2 per cent (including 2 per cent cess) in the Budget, at what rate we have to pay to the Government for the payment realized after that particular date and billing done before that particular date ?

5.If we received a sub-contract from contractor who is charging the service tax to the main contractor, in such case are we exempted for paying service tax on account of double taxation ? What is the exact procedure to get exemption ? What type of documents/letters are required from the employer and or main contractor ?

6.If we give sub-contract to other sub-contractor, can he be exempt from service tax by not charging service tax from us on account of double taxation? What type of document we have to given to that sub-contractor for not charging and ultimately not paying the service tax ?

1. While giving tender ensure that amount stated in the tender is either inclusive of all taxes or it should be clearly mentioned that taxes, if any, would be charged separately. While quoting a figure inclusive of taxes,a note should be stated indicating that any increase in indirect tax rates would be borne by the customer. The Government has issued Notification No. 12/2003-ST, dated June 20, 2003 with effect from July 1, 2003 whereby general exemption has been given from service tax levy on so much of the value of all the taxable services, as is equal to the value of goods and materials sold by the service provider to the recipient of service subject to the condition that there is documentary proof specifically indicating the value of the said goods and materials.

It is further clarified that this exemption would be available only in cases where the sale of such goods is evidenced and the sale value is quantified and shown separately in the invoice.

So, as mentioned above, service tax is not leviable on supply of material, provided the sales value of the material is separately mentioned in the invoice.

In the case of composite contract, where value of material supplied cannot be determined separately, service tax is to be paid at the rate of 8 per cent on 33 per cent of the total composite value.

Let us consider an example :

Value of composite contract 100 (out of which 60 is labour and 40 is material) :

If the invoice shows only the consolidated amount, i.e., Rs. 100, then amount of service tax to be paid would be 8 per cent (100 x 33 per cent) = Rs. 2.64.

If material supply of Rs. 40 is shown separately in the invoice, then service tax to be paid works out to 60 x 8 per cent = Rs. 4.8.

Now let us consider another contract of value Rs. 100 (wherein labour = 20 material = 80) :

If the invoice shows only the consolidated amount, i.e., Rs. 100, then amount of service tax to be paid would be 8 per cent (100 × 33 per cent) = Rs. 2.64.

As I understand, there is 1% Vat in Maharashtra and 0.6% in Gujarat.

In AP VAT the builders have a special option of paying VAT @ 1.25% (Other options are also available).

Vat is payable by builders in Karnataka and Rajasthan for which various scheme are available. Vat is payable in Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal also.

In MP, it seems, the transaction is treated as deemed sale of goods and taxed by excluding value of land. In Haryana, as I understand, builders are not liable to pay State Vat but they have to deduct tax (TDS) and pay to Government. Really, TDS does not mean that Vat is payable by the builder.

It seems in Delhi, department is of the view that Vat is payable but builders are not agreeing on basis of Raheja's case. In any case, they are liable to deduction tax at source on works contract. However, TDS does not mean they are paying State Vat on the works contract.

Thus, in States where the builders/developers are not liable to pay Vat, their service will have to be classified as 'construction' service and not 'works contract' service. The effect would be that they are not entitled to pay service tax under composition scheme of 40%/60%.

However, they can avail 25%/30% abatement scheme if the value includes value of land.

Builders can pay service tax on value of services - Even where builder finds that 25% scheme is not suitable, it does not mean that they have to pay service tax on entire value of works contract. Service tax would still be payable only on value of services. However, in many construction contracts, finding value of service is not easy. In my view, they can still follow the principles of composition scheme, though legally they are not entitled to that scheme.

Builders/Developers liable to pay Vat on construction of residential flats/commercial shops if State law provides - If State Vat Act provides, builders/developers will be liable to pay Vat on construction of residential flats/commercial shops. The issue is discussed in next chapter.

16.2-1 Exemption to sub-contractor providing works contract service to other contractor

Following service is exempt - Sub-contractor providing services by way of works contract to another contractor providing works contract services which are exempt - clause 29(h) Notification No. 25/2012-ST dated 20-6-2012 effective from 1-7-2012.

Thus, if main works contract is exempt, sub-contractor providing works contract service to main contractor will be exempt from service tax. This exemption is only when the sub-contractor provides works contract service and not in other cases.

16.2-2 Sub-contractor liable even if main contractor pays service tax

CBE&C vide circular No. 999.03/23.8.07 has clarified that a sub-contractor is also a taxable service provider. His services are taxable even if these are used by main provider for completion of his work. The sub-contractor is liable even if the service is input service of the main contractor.

Sub-contractor is liable even if main contractor is exempt from service tax - CBE&C circular No. 138/7/2011-ST dated 6-5-2011.

Sub-contractor is liable even if main contractor has paid service tax - Engineers India Technical Services v. CCE (2014) 73 VST 206 (CESTAT).

In Sew Construction Ltd. v. CCE (2011) 32 STT 120 = 12 taxmann.com 12 (CESTAT), it has been held that sub-contractor was liable even prior to 23-8-2007.

However, if sub-contractor is providing a service which is exempt, then he will not be liable e.g. if a contractor is providing works contract service which is exempt and if he entrusts that work to sub-contractor, then the sub-contractor will be providing the works contract service (which is exempt) and hence he will also not be liable to pay service tax. However, if the sub-contractor provides some other service like consultancy, cargo handling, clearing and forwarding which is taxable, then the sub-contractor will be liable to service tax even if the main contractor is exempt - CBE&C circular No. 147/16/2011-ST dated 21-10-2011 (The circular is with reference to works contract service but is applicable to all services provided by sub-contractors).

Sale of ready flat

6. If agreement is to sell ready flat, it is contract of sale of immovable property and would not be liable to service tax.

Contractor or sub-contractor undertaking construction may be liable

7. If a builder/developer gives construction work to a contractor or some finishing work to sub-contractor, such contractor or sub-contractor will be liable. However, if the builder constructs himself, he will not be liable, since service requires two parties. A person cannot give service to himself - In Precot Mills Ltd. v. CCE [2006] 5 STT 35 (CESTAT - Bang.), it was prima facie held that technical assistance provided to its own constituent (another unit of same company) cannot be subjected to service tax, since consultant-client relationship is absent. Hence, stay was granted - view finally confirmed in Precot Mills Ltd.’s case (supra), where it was held that for leviability of service tax, there should be a service provider and service receiver. When one renders service to oneself, there is no question of levy of service tax - same view in Nawanshahr Co-op. Sugar Mills Ltd. v. CCE [2007] 6 STT 18 (CESTAT - New Delhi).

One cannot render service to oneself - In McKinsey & Co. Inc. v. CCE&C [2007] 8 STT 175 (CESTAT - Mum.).

In Rolls Royce Industries Power v. CCE [2004] 6 STT 506 (CESTAT), it was (in effect) held that service tax is attracted when there are two parties. One cannot give service to oneself [The issue was relating to consulting engineering services. It was held that the service is not taxable as there are no two parties, one giving advise and other accepting it].

If the builder/promoter/developer engages petty contractors whose total bill does not exceed exemption limit available to small service providers, the petty contractors will be exempt if their annual bill is less than exemption limit (exactly contrary view in para 2 of same circular!).

SC 2350 = 2 STT 178 = 141 STC 298 (SC), it was held that if a developer enters into contract for construction of residential apartment or unit in commercial complex before construction is completed, he would be liable to pay VAT tax (that time it was sales tax) on the works contract. However, if the agreement is entered into after the flat or unit is already constructed, there would be no works contract. This principle should apply to service tax also. Liability of contractor - Contractor will be liable only if he provides complete service of ‘construction of complex’. simple foundation or RCC work is not ‘construction of complex’. However, in case of finishing services like glazing, plastering, painting, floor and wall tiling, wall covering and wall papering, wood and metal joinery and carpentry, fencing and railing, construction of swimming pools, acoustic applications or fittings and other similar services, the contractor will be liable as finishing services have been specifically included in the definition.

If contractor does not charge service tax, you have no liability, since there is no provision of TDS under service tax.

If the labour contractor is liable and he does not pay service tax, then whether we are in fault ?

Really, service tax will be payable only if you give entire contract of construction to a contractor. In this case, labour contractors for RCC etc. are not liable since they are not providing you service of ‘construction of a complex’. However, in case of finishing services, such services are liable to service tax. In any case, the liability is on the person i.e. contractor who provides the service and not on person who receives the service.

If you sale a flat after construction, then it is contract for sale of flat. It is not a contract for construction of residential complex. However, if you enter into contract prior to that, a view is possible that it is contract for ‘construction of part of residential complex’.

In the above circumstances, whether the developer is liable for service tax on amount received from customers on or after 16-6-2005 or since the construction was started before the applicability of law nothing was liable for tax ?

Really, there is no specific provision in law on this issue. In my view, the developer will be liable to the extent of services provided after 16-6-2005 even if contract was entered prior to 16-6-2005 on proportionate basis. The reason is that what is really relevant for taxation is provision of service and not receipt of advance.

My client is providing service in relation to aluminium panelling of walls with pre-painted/coloured aluminium panels/sheets (a substitute for painting of walls/ decoration of walls) in residential and commercial premises. My client basically takes order in three formats namely (1) contract for fixing of the panels (2) supply of panels and fixing them, at separate rates (3) a consolidated rate contract. My client is however, in no way engaged in construction of new complexes. He acts on the order of owners’ of the premises and some time on the order of builders too. Is my client is subject to Service Tax? If yes, under which category i.e. (a) Construction of residential complex (b) construction service (c) interior decorator’s service? In case if he is liable under category of (a) Construction of residential complex (b) construction service, is he entitled to benefit under NF No. 12/2003, dated 20-6-03 (because vide NF Nos. 15/2004 & 18/2005 abatement of 67% is not available in case of "only completion and finishing service")

He can come under ‘construction of complex’ if the building has more than 12 houses or flats, or when the building is industrial or commercial. Service will not be taxable if service is provided to individual bungalow owner. I agree that 67% abatement will not be available to him. Hence, it is better if he bills separately for material and separately for job charges. This will be convenient for VAT also.

It is seen that the applicant is a developer of Residential Real Estate Project (RREP) for which he has sought the necessary approvals with the relevant authorities. The applicant as a POA of the Landowner, along with the Landowner enters into 'Agreement for Sale' and 'Indenture of Understanding' with the prospective buyer of a Unit of the developed Project and enters into a 'Construction Agreement' with such buyer exclusively. By the clauses of the Construction agreement, it is evident that the prospective buyer does not have a choice to enter into a construction agreement with anyone other than the applicant, i.e., the developer of the project, who undertakes the Construction of the 'Units' and the infrastructure proposed for the project. Thus, it is clear and evident on all fours that the activity of the applicant is construction of a Residential Real Estate Project (RREP) with the infrastructure as approved by the Tamil Nadu RERA and the District Town Planning authorities. The applicant enters into construction agreement with the buyers for their 'Units' in the proposed project along with the agreement for sale and IOU. Thus, the Construction agreement entered into by the applicant with the prospective buyer is not a standalone agreement under which the applicant makes the supply to the customer. The various clauses of the different agreements entered into with the prospective buyer of a 'Unit', mentioned supra establishes that the applicant constructs the RREP; they enter into a construction agreement of a 'Unit' of the said project with the prospective buyer of the said unit along with the agreement for sale, i.e., the construction agreement has been entered into for the 'Unit' with the agreement to sell the same and therefore, there is no merit in the claim of the applicant that the construction of the 'Unit' undertaken by them is not 'intended for sale'. Having established that the construction of the 'Unit' as per the agreements entered into by the applicant with the prospective customer, is to construct the 'unit', which is a part of the RREP developed by them and the construction is undertaken for 'intended sale' before the issue of completion certificate, the activity is a supply taxable under 'GST'. [Para 7.3]

This being the fact, the contentions of the applicant that the activity proposed to be undertaken by them under the 'Construction agreement' entered in respect of the 'Unit' of the prospective buyer constitute a composite supply of works contract are taken up for consideration. They submit that the said activity will involve transfer of property in goods such as cement, steel, mortar etc., to the customer and that the residential unit would qualify as an immovable property without doubt. Thus, they contend that the activity of works contract is by nature a composite supply involving both goods and service which is a sine qua non for a works contract and hence the subject activity is not a contract for services simpliciter. Further they submit that the subject activity would not fall under any of the description of the entry Sl. No. 3 corresponding to the Heading 9954 of the Notification No. 11/2017-Central Tax (Rate), dated 28-6-2017 and therefore would merit classification under the residuary entry, Heading 9997 and will be chargeable to CGST at the rate of 9 per cent under Sl. No. 35 of the said Notification. [Para 8.1]

It is clear that the applicant is the developer of the project and is undertaking the construction of 'Group Housing Project' approved as 'Residential Real Estate Project'. As per the market practice in Chennai, Tarnil Nadu, the applicant enters into an 'agreement for Sale'; 'Construction Agreement'; 'Indenture of Understanding' (IOU) and 'Sale Deed' with the buyer of 'Unit' of the Project. When a supply made by the provider to the receiver is based on more than one agreement, all such agreements are to be considered in a wholesome way to understand the intention of the supply made to the receiver and each agreement cannot be lineated and considered, as handed down by various Juris-prudence. As stated by the applicant, in the case at hand, the Modus proposed to be followed is to enter into an agreement for sale and a construction agreement, both covered under an IOU all executed simultaneously, followed by registration of 'sale deed' executed for the UDS and 'construction agreement' for construction of the 'Unit'. (3) For the purpose of sub-rule (1), the cost of land, if any, in a civil works contract carried on by the builder for the intended purchaser, shall be determined in the following manner:

(a)

Where separate conveyance/sale deed of the land has been executed between the builder and the intended purchaser, the consideration amount of land stated in that deed;

(b)

Where separate conveyance/sale deed of the land has not been executed for transfer of land between the builder and the intended purchaser, then the value of land in the value of composite works contract inclusive of land may be arrived at on any of the following basis:-

(i)

Where proportionate land is transferred by the land-owner to the builder by executing a conveyance/sale deed: On the basis of rate of land arrived at from such deed for the purpose of payment of stamp duty.

(ii)

Where clause (i) is not applicable, on the basis of rate of land arrived at by adding the amount paid by the builder through account payee cheque/draft/pay order/electronic transfer to the land-owner towards the land rights and value of construction transferred by the builder to the land-owner determined as per sub-rule (1A).

To illustrate, land-owner and builder enter into an agreement, where builder would build four units, which would be shared equally between them. In addition, builder pays Rs.1 crore to the land owner. Total construction cost for four flats is Rs.4 crores. Here, builder transfers the value of construction worth Rs. 2 crores [Rs.4 crores divided by two, since 50% share in the construction is transferred to the land-owner]. In this case, value of land transferred by the land-owner is: Rs.1 crore + Rs.2 crores = Rs.3 crores; and total value of land transferred by the builder to the intended purchasers for his share of the land shall also be Rs.3 crores (Rs. 1.5 crs. per flat if there are two intended purchasers).

(iii)

In all other cases where clauses (i) and (ii) are not applicable, the value of land shall be determined on the basis of notified circle rates of land prevailing at the time of execution of agreement between the builder and the intended purchaser.

Provided that where separate circle rates for land and construction have not been notified in respect of certain properties, then circle rate for land and construction prevailing in that locality for other properties in respect of which separate circle rates have been notified, shall be taken for the purpose of determination of value under this sub-rule.

Provided further that where land has been valued at circle rate and the value of conveyance/sale deed with the intended purchaser exceeds the circle rate, then the difference between the two shall be proportionately divided between the value of land and the works contract (comprising material and services).

For example, in case of composite works contract, circle rate of land is Rs.2 crore and circle rate of construction is Rs.1 crore respectively, and the consolidated value of sale deed (inclusive of land and cost of construction) is Rs.3.60 crores. Difference of Rs.0.60 crore shall be divided in the ratio of 2:1; and thus, value of land for the purpose of this sub-rule shall be Rs.2.40 crores.

Judgment in the case L&T

2. The sales tax thrust on builders and developers has gained drastic momentum post the recent rulings of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Larsen & Tubro Ltd. (supra) which, in principle, accepts the law laid down in the earlier judgment in case of K. Raheja Development Corpn. v. State of Karnataka [2005] 2 STT 178 (SC) (Two Judge Bench) and lays a few essential laws as under :-

(a)

Any agreement entered into by the builder / promoter before the completion of construction tantamounts to works contract and, hence, is liable to Value Added Tax (VAT)/ sales tax.

(b)

When an agreement is entered into between the promoter/developer and the flat purchaser to construct a flat and eventually sell the flat with the fraction of land, it is obvious that such transaction involves the activity of construction inasmuch as it is only when the flat is constructed then it can be conveyed. The said activity will be covered by the term "works contract". The term "works contract" is nothing but a contract in which one of the parties is obliged to undertake or to execute works. Such activity of construction has all the characteristics or elements of a works contract.

(c)

In tripartite agreement between the owner of the land, the developer and the flat purchaser, there is nothing wrong if the transaction is treated as a composite contract comprising of both a works contract and a transfer of immovable property and levy sales tax on the value of the material involved in execution of the works contract.

Circular issued by Haryana VAT authorities based on Judgment in L&T's case

3. Based on above, Haryana VAT Authorities have released several circulars on back to back basis in this regard:-

(a)

Even prior to L&T's Judgment, the Haryana VAT Authorities (in conformity with K. Raheja Law) had released Circular No. 952/ST-1, dated 7th May, 2013:-

(i)

This circular clarified the assessment mechanism and various other issues as relevant for taxing such transactions related to agreements by developers/builders with prospective buyers.

(ii)

This circular categorically mentioned that where the builder/developer opts for composition scheme under Rule 49 then the value of taxable consideration shall exclude the land component, except in cases of joint development agreement.

(iii)

Currently, with no other clarification available or legal support under the specific scenario of civil works contract and their relevant ancillary issues like WCT, Valuation, procedural compliances and composition scheme (under Rule 49 as applicable to works contractors), the above said circular can be seen as only legal reference point for builder community.

(b)

Circular No. 693/ST-1, dated 26.3.2013 clarified that the VAT D-1 benefit is available only to manufacturer and lumpsum dealer under Rule 49. Hence, where a Builder/Developer does not opt for composition scheme the benefit of reduced rate under VAT D-1 shall not be available.

(c)

This was followed by another Circular No. 1166/ST-1, dated 4-6-2013 which clarified the limitation aspects in regard to both, the registered dealers and unregistered dealers under sections 15 and 16 of the HVAT, 2003 respectively. Further, the reassessment under section 17 and revision of original order under section 34 have been detailed.

(d)

Circular No. 41/ST-1, dated 14-1-2014 wherein it was clarified that the levy of additional tax @ 5% (i.e. surcharge) is applicable on all the composition rates except that of the retailers. Hence, the effective rate of tax for the works contract dealers / Builders and Developers shall be 4.2%.

(e)

Circular No. 259/ST-1, dated 10-2-2014 takes a stand exactly opposite to Circular No. 952/ST-1 in regard to valuation of taxable consideration under composition scheme. This circular amends the earlier circular to include even the value of land in the value of taxable consideration.
